title: Custom Response Classes
subtopics: Trade-offs when returning a Response directly
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of custom response classes in a FastAPI application.
Apply or interpret one example related to returning a jsonresponse.
Identify one limitation or failure case and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson covers custom response classes within responses, errors, and validation. Use the supplied syllabus topics as the coverage checklist, then connect them to the worked example and the verification task.
content.why_it_matters: You will use custom response classes to build APIs whose contracts and behavior are understandable to both clients and maintainers. The practical aim is clear input/output contracts, field validation, serialization and safe defaults.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Custom Response Classes matters because it is part of responses, errors, and validation. In practice, focus on clear input/output contracts, field validation, serialization and safe defaults. A framework feature only helps when its assumptions match the application; keep input validation, business policy and side effects distinguishable.

items.title: Streaming responses
items.text: For streaming responses, identify which operation waits on I/O, which resources remain open, and what happens on timeout or disconnect. Async syntax does not make CPU-bound work faster or durable background jobs reliable by itself.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Custom Response Classes
content_blocks.run_instructions: Try one existing-style ID and the documented missing-resource case.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For read-only examples, no reset is needed. For any example that writes state, use a disposable local database/test fixture; record the starting state and clean up only lab data. Never use production credentials or real personal data.
content_blocks.limitations: This code is inspectable lesson material, not executed by CodeLeaf. Run it only in a local virtual environment or a separately isolated runner with resource/time/network limits. Security examples are sketches, not complete production authentication or authorization systems.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Adapt the example to cover “Returning a JSONResponse”. Write down the expected success result and one invalid, missing, duplicate, timeout or permission-boundary case that matters for this topic.

task: Create a small reviewable artifact for “Custom Response Classes”: explain its goal, cover the listed subtopics, show an example with expected result, then include one edge case and how you would verify it.
hints: Start with “Returning a JSONResponse” and state the required inputs, output and assumptions.
Change one thing at a time; check the official reference and capture the actual response/error instead of guessing.
Include a negative/edge-case check and document which behavior remains untested.
expected_output: A reviewable example or design note for Custom Response Classes, covering the PDF subtopics, expected behavior and at least one verification check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a code fragment without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Installed versions, imported types, application structure and external services affect behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: State assumptions; check the versioned official docs; run a minimal local test and add one failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one happy-path response as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid input, permissions, concurrency, timeouts and cleanup are not exercised by a single request.
common_mistakes.fix: Add focused normal and negative tests and record exact expected status/body.

common_mistakes.why: Even short examples may mutate records, reveal data or affect availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic inputs and a disposable environment; review security, cleanup and rollback before promotion.

summary: Custom Response Classes belongs to the broader goal of clear input/output contracts, field validation, serialization and safe defaults.
